claims.text: A Pod is isolated for egress when at least one NetworkPolicy selects it with Egress in policyTypes; it may then open only connections allowed by the egress list of some policy that selects it.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Concepts > Services, Load Balancing, and Networking > Network Policies > The two sorts of pod isolation

claims.text: A NetworkPolicy with podSelector: {}, policyTypes [Egress] and no egress list denies every outgoing connection of every Pod in its namespace.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Policies > Default policies > Default deny all egress traffic

claims.text: Egress policies are additive like ingress ones: what all policies selecting a Pod allow is combined, and their order does not matter.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Policies > The two sorts of pod isolation (policies are additive; order of evaluation does not affect the result)

claims.text: For a connection from one Pod to another to be allowed, both the egress policies of the source Pod and the ingress policies of the destination Pod must allow it.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Policies > The two sorts of pod isolation (both the egress policy on the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection)

claims.text: A to entry holding both namespaceSelector and podSelector selects Pods matching the podSelector in namespaces matching the namespaceSelector (both must match); kubernetes.io/metadata.name is set on every namespace to its name.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Policies > Behavior of to and from selectors; Targeting a Namespace by its name; Well-Known Labels > kubernetes.io/metadata.name

claims.text: The CoreDNS Pods run in kube-system with the label k8s-app: kube-dns on kind; after allow-dns-egress.yaml (UDP and TCP 53 to those Pods) client resolves echo-ip again.
claims.source_hint: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns on donhang; examples/don-hang outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/egress-policy.txt lines 11-14

claims.text: DNS runs over both UDP and TCP on port 53; a client sends a query over UDP and falls back to TCP when the answer is too large for UDP.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Tasks > Debugging DNS Resolution (TCP fallback for answers above 512 bytes); RFC 1035 section 4.2

claims.text: A rule's port is a port on the target Pod (NetworkPolicyPort.port), and a policy cannot name a Service. On donhang (kindnet) the policy sees the connection after kube-proxy's rewrite: a rule to app=echo-ip port 80 times out, port 8080 works.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io API reference NetworkPolicyPort (port on a pod); Network Policies > What you can't do (targeting services by name); outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/egress-policy.txt lines 18-24

claims.text: Service echo-ip sends port 80 of its cluster IP to targetPort 8080 of its Pods.
On donhang a connection a NetworkPolicy drops is not refused: the caller gets no answer and gives up at its own timeout (wget -T 5: 'download timed out'; bash /dev/tcp under timeout 5: exit 124).
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/egress-policy.txt lines 15-16, 37-38; DECISIONS.md repo-stage 3 notes (kindnet enforces egress, timeout)

claims.text: Captured on donhang: after deny-egress.yaml getent hosts echo-ip does not resolve; after allow-dns-egress.yaml it resolves and wget to echo-ip times out; with the rule patched to 8080 echo-ip answers.

Staging's base/egress-policies.yaml: default-deny-egress, dns-egress, api-egress (db 5432, redis 6379, rabbitmq 5672, keycloak 8080), payments-egress, notifications-egress, db-clients-egress (migration hooks and db-backup to db 5432).
The api fetches the keys that check tokens from Keycloak on port 8080 (Keycloak__MetadataAddress).
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang deploy/gitops/config-repo-kustomize/base/egress-policies.yaml lines 39-41 at stage-3; DECISIONS.md (api calls Keycloak at http://keycloak:8080)

claims.text: Before the egress policies an api Pod connects to gitea.git port 3000; after commit and Argo CD sync, bash's /dev/tcp under timeout 5 gives no connection (exit 124), signed-in GET /api/v1/orders/1 HTTP 200, 0 Pods whose first container is not ready.
claims.source_hint: outputs/stage-3/scripts/k8s/egress-policy.txt lines 26-61; scripts/k8s/egress-policy.sh reach_git and last line (jsonpath containerStatuses[0].ready)

claims.text: Egress policies apply to connections a Pod opens; reply traffic on an allowed connection is implicitly allowed. The kubelet runs probes from the node and pulls images on the Pod's behalf, and traffic from the Pod's node is always allowed.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Policies (reply traffic; node traffic always allowed); Secrets (kubelet pulls on behalf of the Pod); Pod Lifecycle > Container probes

claims.text: Applying only allow-dns-egress.yaml (Egress in policyTypes, podSelector: {}) isolates every Pod in network-lessons for egress, so wget to echo-ip times out (kubectl exec adds 'command terminated with exit code 1') while DNS works. Not captured.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Policies > The two sorts of pod isolation; deploy/k8s/lessons/allow-dns-egress.yaml

claims.text: client runs caddy:2.10.0 with sleep 3600 in network-lessons; its image has wget and getent. getent hosts asks the resolver for a name; wget -T 5 -qO- prints the body, giving up after 5 s. show/try_name/try_echo are the script's helpers.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang scripts/lib/network-lessons.sh show, client_up; scripts/k8s/egress-policy.sh try_name, try_echo; deploy/k8s/lessons/echo-ip.yaml at stage-3

claims.text: Keeping an explicit deny-all egress policy next to the allow policies is worth it when you want the Pods to stay isolated even if an allow policy (such as the DNS one) is removed.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Network Policies > Default deny all egress traffic; staging's base/egress-policies.yaml
